newsitem.title: JAPAN: Judge refuses to excuse Japan cult guru from court.
newsitem.headline: Judge refuses to excuse Japan cult guru from court.

text.p: The doomsday cult guru accused of a deadly nerve gas attack on the Tokyo subway failed in an attempt to be excused from his murder trial on Thursday by saying he was sick.
After sitting quietly for about 30 minutes, Shoko Asahara began making periodic outbursts and demanded that the chief judge allow him to leave the courtroom.
"I want you to let the defendant leave the courtroom because he is sick and has a fever," a defence lawyer told chief judge Fumihiro Abe after Asahara whispered to him.
But the chief judge refused and told Asahara to remain in the court.
"You must endure it," Abe told Asahara, leader of the Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect).
But Asahara, 41, whose real name is Chizuo Matsumoto, did not give up, saying: "I want to leave because I feel a little bit sick."
Asahara is on trial for murder and other charges for the March 21, 1995, sarin nerve gas attack on Tokyo's subway system which killed 12 people and made 6,000 ill.
The cult leader, stroking his long black beard from time to time, recovered his composure and sat impassively.
In Thursday's testimony, Toru Toyoda, one of the five cultists accused of actually carrying out the subway attack, said he believed Asahara was the mastermind of the gassing.
When asked by prosecutors if he felt Asahara was responsible for the attack, Toyoda said: "I feel the leaders of the cult are very responsible.
"The aim was to deal a telling blow to the police," said Toyada, 28.
The former cult member acknowledged his involvement in the attack and expressed deep repentance.
"As a human being, it was an unforgivable act. When I think of my own evil, even regret is not enough," he said in a clipped, monotone voice.
Apart from the subway attack, Asahara is on trial for a host of other crimes, including another gas attack, kidnapping and murder.
Asahara has not entered a plea. If convicted of murder he could face execution by hanging.
Recently, Asahara has gone into fits of uncontrolled rage during his trial at the Tokyo District Court when key disciples testified against him.
More that 100 other members of the cult are also on trial in connection with its activities.
